paragraphs: Network embedding methods assign each node a vector so that standard learning methods can use network information for tasks such as node classification and link prediction. This paper studies what happens when methods such as DeepWalk and node2vec also penalize the squared sizes of those vectors. The question is what this familiar regularization choice means for the network structure being learned.

Under exchangeability assumptions on the graph, the authors prove an asymptotic connection to learning a graphon with a nuclear-norm-type penalty. They also provide guarantees describing the asymptotic distribution of the embedding vectors. Crucially, the resulting penalty depends on how graph samples are selected during stochastic gradient descent: the sampling procedure helps determine the effect of regularization.

The paper also empirically examines combining regularized node2vec embeddings with node attributes by simply concatenating them. This achieves comparable, and sometimes better, performance than methods that combine attributes and network structure nonlinearly. The findings give theoretical meaning to embedding regularization while supporting a relatively simple way to incorporate additional node information.
neurips-2022-asymptotics-of-ell-2-regula.tldr: Under graph exchangeability assumptions, squared-vector regularization induces a sampling-dependent structural penalty on network embeddings.

paragraphs: A neural network can fit its training data extremely closely and still perform well on unseen examples. This phenomenon, called benign overfitting, complicates the idea that fitting the training set too well necessarily damages generalization. The paper investigates when this behavior occurs in a two-layer convolutional neural network, extending theoretical analysis beyond linear models and kernel or random-feature models.

The authors analyze training by gradient descent and identify a condition on the signal-to-noise ratio. When that condition holds, the network can reach arbitrarily small losses on both training and test data. When it does not hold, the resulting network retains a constant level of test loss, making the overfitting harmful in the analyzed setting.

Together, these results characterize a sharp transition between two different outcomes of fitting the training data. The signal-to-noise ratio determines which regime occurs under the paper's analysis. The contribution is a precise theoretical account for the studied convolutional network, connecting successful generalization to the balance between useful signal and noise rather than training fit alone.
neurips-2022-benign-overfitting-in-two-l.tldr: The paper characterizes a signal-to-noise-driven transition between benign and harmful overfitting in a two-layer CNN trained by gradient descent.

paragraphs: Compositional generalization means handling unfamiliar combinations of concepts that were individually observed during training. This paper tests whether unsupervised methods designed to organize representations into meaningful components actually support that ability. Its evaluation asks whether a simple model trained on a learned representation can generalize to new combinations, rather than judging only how structured the representation appears.

The authors compare beta-VAE, beta-TCVAE, and emergent-language autoencoders on two datasets. With simple downstream models and few labels, the central bottleneck representation can generalize worse than representations from layers before or after it. Previously proposed compositionality metrics also fail to correlate with compositional generalization within this evaluation framework.

Increasing pressure for disentanglement produces worse generalization in the reported study, while emergent-language representations generalize strongly. Those models consistently outperform the disentanglement models, particularly with less unlabeled training data and fewer downstream labels. The findings support testing representations through their downstream ability to recombine concepts and suggest benefits from further developing emergent-language learning methods.
neurips-2022-compositional-generalizatio.tldr: In the studied setting, emergent-language representations generalize to new concept combinations better than disentanglement models, and compositionality metrics do not predict that ability.

paragraphs: Graph classifiers can learn misleading relationships between graph patterns and labels. In an investigation with severely biased training graphs, the authors find that graph neural networks favor these spurious relationships even when causal information is available. Their causal analysis identifies two important steps for addressing this problem: separating causal information from bias and reducing the correlation between them.

The proposed framework learns an edge mask that divides each input graph into causal and bias subgraphs. Separate graph neural networks encode these parts, using losses tailored to their respective roles. The resulting representations also support the synthesis of counterfactual training samples intended to reduce the remaining association between causal and bias variables.

To evaluate severe bias more directly, the authors construct three graph datasets with adjustable bias levels and structures that are easier to visualize and explain. Experiments report better generalization than existing baselines. The learned edge masks also provide interpretability and transferability, connecting the prediction process to explicit graph substructures rather than leaving the separation entirely inside hidden representations.
neurips-2022-debiasing-graph-neural-netw.tldr: The method separates causal and bias subgraphs and generates counterfactual training samples to improve graph-classification generalization under severe bias.

paragraphs: Active learning selects examples for labeling so that a model can learn effectively from the selected data. For deep networks, many selection rules rely on empirical intuition rather than theoretical justification. This paper develops dynamicAL, a method that chooses samples according to training dynamics, linking the selection decision to how learning progresses.

The theoretical argument connects training convergence speed with generalization performance. Under an ultra-wide-network condition, the authors prove a positive correlation between the two and show that maximizing the training dynamics improves generalization. This condition matters: the formal connection is established in that regime, giving the selection rule a specific theoretical foundation.

The authors also introduce two relaxations of the subset-selection problem to make the method usable with large networks and datasets. They report reducing the selection problem's time complexity from polynomial to constant. Empirically, dynamicAL consistently outperforms the compared baselines and scales well to large deep learning models. The work therefore combines a theory-motivated selection criterion with computational changes that support its practical use.
neurips-2022-deep-active-learning-by-lev.tldr: dynamicAL uses a theoretically motivated connection between training dynamics and generalization to select informative samples efficiently.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer sparse computation and temporal dynamics, but architectures borrowed from conventional neural networks may not suit them well. This paper introduces SpikeDHS to search for architectures using spike-based computation at both the cell and layer levels. The aim is to find effective designs within limited computational cost as tasks demand different structures.

The method also searches for surrogate gradient functions used during training. A poorly chosen surrogate can approximate the true gradient badly and steer optimization into certain local minima. The authors extend their differentiable search approach to optimize the surrogate locally, addressing both network structure and the training signal used to fit it.

The resulting models report state-of-the-art classification performance on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet, with accuracies of 95.50%, 76.25%, and 68.64%. On event-based deep stereo, the searched model surpasses specially designed conventional networks in accuracy while using 26 times less energy, at 6.7 mJ. These findings support the usefulness of adapting spiking architectures and training functions, particularly for sparse, dynamic inputs.
neurips-2022-differentiable-hierarchical.tldr: SpikeDHS searches spiking-network architectures and surrogate gradients, reporting strong classification results and energy-efficient event-based stereo.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover a hidden component from data containing a mixture of two components. Its setting makes two central assumptions: the components are statistically independent, and the mixing process is invertible. One component is observed, while the other is hidden. That observed component supplies additional information for the recovery problem.

The authors propose an autoencoder equipped with a discriminator. They show that, in this special case of independent component analysis, their approach can recover the hidden component up to an entropy-preserving transformation. The qualification describes the recovery guarantee: it allows a transformed version of the component, rather than requiring its exact original form.

This result addresses a setting distinct from standard nonlinear independent component analysis, which is non-identifiable. The paper demonstrates the proposed approach on image synthesis, voice cloning, and fetal ECG extraction. Together, the theory and demonstrations show how observing one independent component can make hidden-component discovery possible under the stated mixing assumptions, across several different kinds of data.
neurips-2022-discovery-of-single-indepen.tldr: Given an invertible mixture of two independent components with one observed, the method can recover the hidden component up to an entropy-preserving transformation.

paragraphs: Computational imaging can jointly optimize an optical system and a neural network that reconstructs images from its measurements. Some applications require optical encoders that mix information across distant locations. The paper identifies a locality bias in existing deep decoders that prevents effective optimization of these highly non-local encoders, including those needed to compress a 3D volume into one 2D image.

The authors introduce FourierNets, shallow reconstruction networks using global-kernel Fourier convolutions. Their broad spatial operations address the mismatch between non-local optical measurements and locally biased decoders. FourierNets outperform existing deep-network decoders when reconstructing photographs captured with the highly non-local DiffuserCam encoder.

The method also enables joint optimization of non-local encoders for 3D snapshot microscopy. Combined with a large, multi-GPU differentiable optical simulation, it supports encoders reported to be 170 to 7,372 times larger than prior state of the art. A programmable-microscope demonstration further shows potential for optical encoding tailored to particular region-of-interest types. The results connect decoder design to which optical systems can be optimized.
neurips-2022-fouriernets-enable-the-desi.tldr: FourierNets use global convolutions to reconstruct non-local optical measurements and enable optimization of much larger computational-imaging encoders.

paragraphs: GAUDI is a generative model for complex 3D scenes that can be viewed from a moving camera. The task involves representing both what a scene looks like and the camera poses from which it is rendered. The paper addresses these together while separating their contributions within a learned latent representation.

Its approach first optimizes a representation that disentangles radiance fields and camera poses. A generative model is then learned using that representation, supporting both unrestricted generation and generation guided by additional information. The method removes the assumption that all samples share a camera-pose distribution, generalizing earlier approaches focused on individual objects.

The authors report state-of-the-art unconditional generation performance across multiple datasets. They also show conditional scene generation from sparse image observations or descriptive text. These results indicate that the same overall approach can model scene variation and respond to different forms of guidance. Separating scene content from camera poses is central to extending generation toward immersive scenes with differing viewing configurations.
neurips-2022-gaudi-a-neural-architect-fo.tldr: GAUDI separates scene and camera representations to generate immersive 3D scenes unconditionally or from sparse images and text.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains an agent from a fixed dataset, yet the agent may need to handle situations absent from training. Self-supervised signals have helped generalization in online learning, but those approaches can struggle when transferred to the offline setting. This paper identifies poor estimates of similarity between observations as a reason for that difficulty.

The proposed Generalized Similarity Functions framework uses contrastive learning to group observations according to their expected future behavior. Generalized value functions quantify that similarity. This makes the representation-learning objective sensitive to how observations relate to future behavior, providing a basis for deciding which observations should be represented together.

The framework is theoretically motivated and broad enough to recover existing self-supervised objectives. On two complex benchmarks where offline agents learn from pixels, it improves zero-shot generalization performance. The findings connect the success of auxiliary representation learning to the quality and meaning of its similarity signal, and show that behavior-based similarity can improve transfer to unseen scenarios in the evaluated offline tasks.
neurips-2022-improving-zero-shot-general.tldr: Generalized Similarity Functions improve offline RL generalization by learning observation representations based on similarity in expected future behavior.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning the distribution of a sum of independent integer-valued random variables whose possible values are unbounded. It asks when learning can avoid dependence on the number of summands or the largest possible value. It also studies sparse covers: collections of distributions that approximate the relevant family in total variation distance.

The authors give sufficient conditions for learning such sums with sample complexity polynomial in the inverse error tolerance. For unimodal distributions in exponential families satisfying structural assumptions, they also address proper sparse covers. These assumptions permit some heavy-tailed and non-log-concave distributions, extending the scope beyond more restrictive distribution shapes.

For qualifying families with k parameters, the learning guarantee uses roughly linear dependence on k, up to logarithmic factors, multiplied by a polynomial in inverse accuracy. The output remains a sum of distributions from the same family. An intermediate result shows that suitable moment bounds allow approximation using a bounded portion of an otherwise unbounded parameter space, helping make these infinite families manageable.
neurips-2022-learning-and-covering-sums-.tldr: Under structural assumptions, sums of unbounded integer-valued variables can be learned accurately with sample requirements independent of the number of summands.

paragraphs: A video's text description rarely explains every frame. Some frames show other content, and others contain transitions, teasers, or information irrelevant to the description. This paper argues that treating all extracted frames as semantically aligned with the text introduces noise into video-language modeling, even when attention mechanisms are used.

The Language-Guided Denoising Network uses language supervision to dynamically remove frames that are misaligned or redundant. It retains only two to four salient frames per video for token-level alignment between video and language. Frame selection therefore becomes part of the modeling approach, focusing the cross-modal comparison on a small set of relevant visual observations.

Experiments on five public datasets report large improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The authors also use ablation studies to examine the importance of addressing noise. The findings support explicitly filtering the visual material used for alignment: a compact selection guided by language can provide a stronger basis for video-language modeling than retaining every extracted frame in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2022-lgdn-language-guided-denois.tldr: LGDN uses language to select two to four relevant video frames, improving video-language modeling by removing misaligned and redundant content.

paragraphs: Neural networks can have symmetries built into their architecture, reducing the need to learn those relationships from examples. This paper instead investigates symmetries acquired from data when they have not been specified in advance. Its goal is to reveal which transformations a trained network has learned to treat as leaving its task behavior unchanged.

The proposed method extracts learned invariances as generators of corresponding Lie groups and evaluates how invariant the network is to them. These generators give an explicit representation of the learned symmetries. The extraction does not require prior knowledge of the symmetries in the data, allowing the method to examine what the network actually learned.

The authors use this tool to study how network parameterization and configuration affect symmetry learning. They find this ability across a range of architectures, while the quality of learned symmetries depends on depth and parameter count. The contribution is therefore both an inspection method and evidence that architectural choices influence how well networks acquire invariances from data.
neurips-2022-liegg-studying-learned-lie-.tldr: LieGG extracts and evaluates symmetries learned by neural networks, showing that their quality depends on depth and parameter count.

paragraphs: Online learning algorithms must perform reliably even on difficult sequences, but they can sometimes achieve stronger guarantees when the data is easier. This paper studies that balance when the experts being compared have very different loss ranges. In this multiscale setting, a meaningful regret guarantee should reflect each expert's own range, rather than the largest range among all experts.

The authors develop algorithms, tuning schemes, and analysis techniques that combine worst-case robustness with adaptation to easier data at negligible cost. The motivation includes stronger guarantees available under statistical margin assumptions. Accounting for different scales makes the comparison more sensitive to the particular expert against which performance is measured.

The paper further extends the approach with optimism and applies it to multiscale two-player zero-sum games. Experiments show superior performance for the scale-adaptive algorithm, and the authors discuss its relationship to Freund's open problem. The work connects scale-sensitive guarantees with favorable-data adaptation while retaining protection against difficult online learning sequences.
neurips-2022-luckiness-in-multiscale-onl.tldr: New multiscale online-learning algorithms adapt to easier data while retaining worst-case guarantees that respect each expert's loss range.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from pixels requires an agent to turn large visual observations into useful representations of its state. Limited experience makes that representation-learning problem difficult. This paper introduces an additional self-supervised task intended to extract more useful information from the observations already available to the agent.

Mask-based Latent Reconstruction hides pixels across both space and time and asks the model to predict the complete state representation. The prediction takes place in the latent representation space. Recovering that representation from incomplete observations encourages the model to use contextual information, making the learned state description more informative for reinforcement learning.

Experiments across multiple continuous and discrete control benchmarks report significant improvements in sample efficiency and performance beyond the compared state-of-the-art sample-efficient methods. These findings indicate that the reconstruction task helps agents make better use of limited experience in the evaluated settings. The contribution is a simple auxiliary learning method that connects masked observation modeling directly to the internal representations used to train control agents.
neurips-2022-mask-based-latent-reconstru.tldr: Predicting complete latent states from spatially and temporally masked observations improves sample efficiency in pixel-based reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning asks a neural network to adapt using very little data, where large models can easily overfit. Sparse architectures restrict the set of functions a model can learn, but manually designed structures may still be insufficient. This paper asks whether meta-learning across tasks can discover sparse structures that are particularly effective for learning from few examples.

Meta-ticket searches for sparse subnetworks within randomly initialized neural networks. Its central design choice is to use meta-learning to identify a useful subnetwork structure for few-shot learning. This brings the idea of restricting the model's hypothesis space into a process that learns from multiple tasks rather than relying solely on manual architecture design.

The experiments show that the discovered subnetworks can learn features specialized to each task. The authors connect this task-specific adaptation ability to better meta-generalization than MAML-based methods, especially for large neural networks. The findings support learned sparsity as a promising way to prepare models for new tasks with little data, with the reported advantage established empirically.
neurips-2022-meta-ticket-finding-optimal.tldr: Meta-ticket learns sparse subnetworks inside randomly initialized networks that empirically improve few-shot meta-generalization, especially in large models.

paragraphs: Neural implicit methods reconstruct 3D surfaces from multiple images and often produce smooth, complete results. Their performance can deteriorate for complex scenes or sparse viewpoints because matching image colors leaves the geometry ambiguous. Areas with little texture or few observations are particularly weakly constrained by that objective.

MonoSDF systematically investigates adding depth and surface-normal cues predicted by general-purpose monocular estimators. These cues provide geometric information beyond the RGB reconstruction signal. The authors also compare several ways of representing the surface, including a single multilayer perceptron, a single grid, and grids at multiple resolutions.

The study finds that monocular depth and normal cues significantly improve reconstruction quality and optimization time. Benefits appear for both small scenes containing one object and larger scenes containing multiple objects, across the investigated representation choices. This matters because the useful addition is geometric guidance that works with several surface models. The results support using monocular predictions to constrain ambiguities that image-color matching alone does not adequately resolve.
neurips-2022-monosdf-exploring-monocular.tldr: MonoSDF shows that predicted monocular depth and normals improve neural surface reconstruction quality and optimization time across several representations.

paragraphs: Neural models for tables must decide how to represent each numerical value before combining information across features. Transformer-like models often map individual numbers into larger vectors first. This paper argues that the design of those numerical embeddings is an important, underexplored choice that can substantially affect performance across different neural architectures.

The authors develop two approaches: one represents scalar values through piecewise linear encoding, while the other uses periodic activations. Experiments show that both can substantially improve performance over embeddings built from conventional components such as linear layers and ReLU activations. The improvements therefore come from changing how numerical inputs enter the model.

The benefits extend beyond Transformers. With suitable embeddings, simple MLP-like models can match attention-based architectures, and deep models can compete on some benchmarks that favor gradient boosted decision trees over conventional deep learning. These findings make input representation a significant design consideration when comparing tabular architectures: a relatively simple backbone can become much more competitive when its numerical features are encoded effectively.
neurips-2022-on-embeddings-for-numerical.tldr: Better numerical-feature embeddings can substantially improve tabular neural models and let simple MLP-like architectures match attention-based ones.

paragraphs: Text-guided image editing requires connecting the meaning of a prompt to changes in an image representation. Earlier approaches linking CLIP text embeddings with StyleGAN's visual latent space use mappings that restrict each manipulation model to a fixed prompt. FFCLIP aims to learn that connection automatically so one model can respond to free-form text for a given image category.

Its semantic modulation module first aligns the text and visual spaces using linear transformations and cross-attention. It then injects information from the text embedding into StyleGAN's latent space. This separates the process of establishing a correspondence between modalities from applying the prompt's meaning to the image representation.

The authors evaluate the method on portraits, cars, and churches, reporting semantically accurate and visually realistic edits through visual and numerical results. They also observe edits from prompts combining multiple meanings, although individual training prompts contain only one meaning. The scope remains one learned model per image type, with flexibility across prompts within that type.
neurips-2022-one-model-to-edit-them-all-.tldr: FFCLIP learns to align text and StyleGAN representations so one model per image type can perform edits from free-form prompts.

paragraphs: Open-set recognition requires handling both familiar classes and examples from classes absent during training. Evaluating that combined goal is difficult. This paper analyzes existing metrics and finds that some can give favorable scores when strong familiar-class predictions conceal poor unknown-class handling, while novelty-detection AUC ignores familiar-class classification performance.

The authors propose OpenAUC, a metric with a pairwise formulation that couples the evaluation of known-class and unknown-class performance. This makes the relationship between the two responsibilities part of the evaluation itself. Their analysis shows that OpenAUC avoids the specific inconsistency properties identified in the existing metrics.

The paper also introduces an end-to-end learning method that minimizes OpenAUC risk. Experiments on established benchmark datasets support its effectiveness. The contribution therefore spans both measuring the task and training for that measurement: it aims to align the score and learning objective with the requirement to classify familiar inputs correctly while also dealing successfully with unfamiliar classes.
neurips-2022-openauc-towards-auc-oriente.tldr: OpenAUC jointly evaluates known-class classification and unknown-class handling, avoiding specific inconsistencies in existing open-set recognition metrics.

paragraphs: An online retailer's product ordering affects revenue, but ranking depends on how shoppers browse and buy. This paper studies a model in which customers can purchase multiple products while facing separate limits on viewing and purchasing. Random attention spans determine how many products they view, and random purchase budgets determine how many they buy.

Under this behavioral model, the authors first derive an optimal ranking policy when customer behavior is known precisely. They then develop Multiple-Purchase-with-Budget UCB algorithms for the online setting, where the retailer must estimate that behavior while choosing rankings. Learning customer behavior and earning revenue therefore happen together.

The online algorithms have regret growing on the order of the square root of the number of rounds, up to logarithmic factors. Experiments on synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets support their effectiveness. The theoretical results apply within the stated attention-and-budget model, which explicitly accommodates multiple purchases and bounded browsing. This provides a ranking framework for behavior that simpler single-purchase assumptions do not capture.
neurips-2022-product-ranking-for-revenue.tldr: The paper derives optimal and online-learning product rankings for a customer model with multiple purchases, random attention spans, and purchase budgets.

paragraphs: Topological data analysis describes structural properties that complement conventional analyses, but computing its summaries can be expensive on large networks. This paper develops two graph-reduction algorithms for computing exact persistence diagrams. The aim is to reduce the amount of graph that must be processed while preserving the desired topological result.

The first result proves that a graph's (k+1)-core is sufficient to compute its kth persistence diagram. The second algorithm prunes dominated vertices before computing persistence diagrams. Both approaches use graph structure to identify reductions compatible with exact computation, connecting graph-theoretic operations with the needs of topological analysis.

Experiments on large networks show computational gains of up to 95%. That is a reported maximum gain, rather than a guarantee for every graph. The central significance is that reduced computational work can coexist with exact persistence diagrams. This makes the approach relevant to applying topological methods in machine learning on large, complex networks, where the cost of existing computations can otherwise make analysis infeasible.
neurips-2022-reduction-algorithms-for-pe.tldr: CoralTDA and PrunIT reduce graphs while preserving exact persistence diagrams, with reported computational gains of up to 95%.

paragraphs: This paper revisits stochastic online learning with feedback graphs, focusing on how to judge an algorithm's regret over different time scales. Finite-time performance concerns a limited learning horizon, while asymptotic performance concerns behavior as that horizon grows. The authors seek algorithms with strong guarantees in both senses, up to constant factors.

Their central finding is that optimal finite-time regret is not uniquely defined in this setting. Different choices of the finite-time benchmark matter, and finite-time optimality is generally separate from the asymptotic rate. Consequently, a claim about long-run optimality does not by itself settle what should count as optimal performance at a finite horizon.

The authors examine alternative definitions and propose a notion of finite-time optimality that they argue is meaningful. For that notion, they provide an algorithm with quasi-optimal regret both at finite horizons and asymptotically. The contribution combines clarification of the evaluation target with an algorithmic result: its simultaneous guarantee is tied to the proposed definition of finite-time optimality.
neurips-2022-stochastic-online-learning-.tldr: The paper clarifies finite-time optimality for learning with feedback graphs and gives an algorithm that is quasi-optimal under its proposed notion and asymptotically.

paragraphs: The branching shape of a neuron carries information relevant to cell types, brain development, and neurological changes. Traditional morphology analysis relies heavily on manually chosen features and visual inspection. This paper develops TreeMoCo to learn a quantitative representation of neuron-tree structure without requiring labels for the representation-learning stage.

TreeMoCo uses a Tree-LSTM network to encode morphology and a self-supervised contrastive-learning framework to learn features. The tree-based encoder directly matches the branching form of the input. This approach makes learned representations available for morphology analysis while reducing reliance on a predefined collection of heuristic measurements.

The authors evaluate TreeMoCo on 2,403 high-quality 3D reconstructions of mouse neurons collected from three public resources. They find it effective for both classifying major brain cell types and identifying subtypes. These results support the usefulness of the learned features for distinguishing neuronal forms at different levels of detail. The paper presents contrastive representation learning as a promising direction for more quantitative neuron-morphology analysis.
neurips-2022-treemoco-contrastive-neuron.tldr: TreeMoCo learns neuron-shape representations without labels and shows effectiveness in identifying major cell types and subtypes from mouse neuron reconstructions.

paragraphs: Visual prompting asks a pretrained model to infer a new image-to-image task from examples supplied at test time. The examples show input images and their desired outputs, alongside a new input that needs an output. This paper investigates doing so without task-specific fine-tuning or changes to the model.

The approach arranges the examples and new input into one combined image, leaving a hole where the new output should appear. An image-inpainting model fills that hole. The authors find this effective when the model has been trained on suitable data, and train masked autoencoders on a curated collection of 88,000 unlabeled figures from academic papers on arXiv.

The pretrained models demonstrate visual prompting on foreground segmentation, single-object detection, colorization, edge detection, and other image-to-image tasks. The examples communicate the desired transformation through their arrangement in the prompt. The findings show that an inpainting formulation can support adaptation across these tasks, while emphasizing that the choice of pretraining data is important to making the approach work.
neurips-2022-visual-prompting-via-image-.tldr: A suitably pretrained inpainting model can use visual input-output examples to perform new image tasks without task-specific fine-tuning.
